prompt: Two short reaches (A and B) of the same river were observed during one controlled flood. The same flood hydrograph passed both reaches (so local shear-stress–time history is the same). At each reach operators provided identical tagged clasts in abundant supply: spherical-equivalent diameters 5.0 cm, 8.0 cm, and 12.0 cm. Observers recorded which tagged clasts were mobilized (a clast counted as mobilized if displaced at least one channel width). Results: Reach A—5.0 cm, 8.0 cm, and 12.0 cm clasts were mobilized. Reach B—5.0 cm and 8.0 cm clasts were mobilized; 12.0 cm clasts remained stationary. Using the operational definition that competence equals the maximum particle size actually mobilized when availability is controlled, which conclusion is best supported by these observations?

choices.A: Reach A has greater competence than Reach B.
choices.B: Reach B has greater competence than Reach A.
choices.C: Reaches A and B have equal competence (both mobilized the same maximum size).
choices.D: Competence cannot be determined from these observations because discharge or bed texture measurements are needed.

solution_steps: Apply the operational definition: competence = largest size actually mobilized when availability is controlled (same flood, identical clasts available).
Compare largest mobilized sizes: Reach A mobilized 12.0 cm; Reach B mobilized only 8.0 cm. Therefore Reach A has greater competence.
solution: Given the controlled conditions: same flood hydrograph at both reaches and identical, abundant tagged clasts (5.0, 8.0, 12.0 cm) with identical shape and density and equal placement opportunity, competence is operationally measured as the largest particle size actually mobilized. Observations show Reach A mobilized the 12.0 cm clast while Reach B did not (B mobilized up to 8.0 cm). Therefore Reach A demonstrated a higher competence than Reach B.

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: Two short reaches of the same river are observed during a single controlled flood where identical sets of tagged clasts are made available at both reaches.
fixed_givens: Same flood hydrograph passed both reaches (same shear stress/time history).
At each reach operators placed identical tagged clasts in abundant supply: 5.0 cm, 8.0 cm, and 12.0 cm diameter (spherical-equivalent) clasts.
Observers recorded which tagged clasts were actually mobilized during that flood at each reach.
Reach A: 5.0 cm, 8.0 cm, and 12.0 cm tagged clasts were mobilized.
Reach B: 5.0 cm and 8.0 cm tagged clasts were mobilized; 12.0 cm remained stationary.
Definition: competence = the maximum particle size a stream can move under given flow conditions (operationally measured as the largest size actually mobilized when availability is controlled).
assumptions: Tagged clasts are identical in shape and density at both reaches.
Bed-availability and placement ensured equal opportunity for each size to be entrained at both reaches (no hiding or supply bias).
Mobilization is unambiguous: a clast is considered mobilized if it was displaced at least one channel width during the flood.
solution_steps: Apply the operational definition: competence equals the largest size actually mobilized under the same flood when availability is controlled.
Compare largest mobilized sizes: Reach A mobilized 12.0 cm; Reach B mobilized only 8.0 cm. Therefore Reach A has greater competence.
solution_first_blueprint.expected_answer: Reach A has greater competence (because it mobilized the 12.0 cm clast while Reach B did not).
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: Given identical flood, identical clast availability, and unambiguous mobilization records, the largest mobilized size uniquely determines which reach had greater competence; no other measured outcome is needed to decide between A and B.
distractor_mechanisms: Choose the reach with coarser deposited bed (misuse of D50 as competence indicator) — leads to incorrect inference because deposit statistics are not controlled or unique.
Choose the reach with higher instantaneous discharge reported upstream (confuses discharge with local competence without mobilization evidence).
Choose the reach with visually rougher bed texture (appeal to appearance/hiding effects rather than direct mobilization of identical test clasts).

prompt: Two measured cross sections (Upstream and Downstream) of the same steady stream have identical discharge but different channel areas and mean velocities. Given: steady flow so Q = A·v; Upstream A_u = 4.00 m^2, v_u = 0.50 m/s; Downstream A_d = 2.00 m^2, v_d = 1.00 m/s. Capacity (mass transport rate) is Capacity = C·Q with C = 0.50 kg/m^3. Competence (maximum movable particle diameter) is D_max = K·v^2 with K = 40.0 mm/(m^2/s^2). Assume sediment supply is sufficient and v is the relevant velocity for competence. Based on these relations and values, which stream property primarily determines which section can move the larger individual pebble?

choices.A: Capacity — the section with greater mass transport rate (kg/s) can move the larger pebble.
choices.B: Competence — the section with the higher mean velocity (and thus higher v^2) can move the larger pebble.
choices.C: Both capacity and competence equally determine the largest pebble size since discharge is the same.
choices.D: Chemical/dissolved load controls pebble release, so neither capacity nor competence governs maximum pebble diameter here.

solution_steps: Compute discharge Q for each cross section using Q = A·v and compare.
Compute capacity (mass rate) at each cross section: Capacity = C·Q and compare.
Compute competence D_max at each cross section using D_max = K·v^2 (in mm) and compare.
Decide which property controls the largest movable particle based on the comparisons.
solution: Step 1—Discharge: Q_u = A_u·v_u = 4.00 m^2·0.50 m/s = 2.00 m^3/s. Q_d = A_d·v_d = 2.00 m^2·1.00 m/s = 2.00 m^3/s. Discharge is equal. Step 2—Capacity: Capacity_u = C·Q_u = 0.50 kg/m^3·2.00 m^3/s = 1.00 kg/s. Capacity_d = 0.50·2.00 = 1.00 kg/s. Capacities are equal. Step 3—Competence: D_max,u = K·v_u^2 = 40.0·(0.50^2) = 40.0·0.25 = 10.0 mm. D_max,d = 40.0·(1.00^2) = 40.0·1.00 = 40.0 mm. Downstream can move much larger particles. Step 4—Conclusion: Because discharge and thus capacity are identical while D_max differs (depends on v^2), competence (velocity-squared dependence) primarily determines which section can move the larger pebble. Therefore answer B.

point_breakdown.1: 1 point — Correctly compute and state that Q_u = Q_d = 2.00 m^3/s and Capacity_u = Capacity_d = 1.00 kg/s (shows capacity equality).
point_breakdown.2: 1 point — Correctly compute D_max,u = 10.0 mm and D_max,d = 40.0 mm and conclude competence controls the larger particle (selects B).

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: Two measured cross sections (Upstream, Downstream) of the same steady stream with identical discharge but different channel area and velocity; students must use explicit numeric relations to decide which stream property controls the maximum pebble diameter transported.
fixed_givens: Steady flow: discharge Q is the same at both cross sections.
Upstream cross section: area A_u = 4.00 m^2, mean velocity v_u = 0.50 m/s.
Downstream cross section: area A_d = 2.00 m^2, mean velocity v_d = 1.00 m/s.
Discharge relation: Q = A * v (use these A and v to compute Q).
Capacity relation (given): Capacity_mass_rate = C * Q, with C = 0.50 kg/m^3. Capacity has units kg/s and measures total mass transport potential per time.
Competence relation (given): D_max (largest particle diameter movable) = K * v^2, with K = 40.0 mm / (m^2/s^2). D_max is in mm and depends on mean flow velocity squared.
assumptions: Sediment supply is sufficient at both cross sections so transport is limited by hydraulic ability, not lack of sediment.
Mean velocity v represents the relevant shear-producing velocity for competence (no correction factors needed).
Units are consistent: compute Q in m^3/s, capacity in kg/s, and D_max in mm using the given K.
solution_steps: Compute discharge Q at each cross section using Q = A * v; show equality or difference.
Compute Capacity_mass_rate = C * Q at each cross section and compare.
Compute D_max at each cross section: D_max = K * v^2 (calculate numerical mm values) and compare.
Decide which stream property (capacity or competence) primarily determines the largest particle diameter based on the computed comparisons.
solution_first_blueprint.expected_answer: B — Competence. Calculations: Q_u = 4.00*0.50 = 2.00 m^3/s; Q_d = 2.00*1.00 = 2.00 m^3/s (discharge equal). Capacity_u = Capacity_d = 0.50*2.00 = 1.00 kg/s (same capacity). D_max_u = 40.0*(0.50^2) = 10.0 mm; D_max_d = 40.0*(1.00^2) = 40.0 mm (downstream moves larger particles). Because D_max scales with v^2 and velocities differ while Q (and thus capacity) is equal, competence controls the largest particle diameter (units mm).
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: Discharge (and thus capacity) is identical at both sections, so capacity cannot explain the observed difference in largest movable particle; only competence (which depends on v^2 and differs numerically between sections) predicts the different D_max values—hence the choice is uniquely determined by the provided measurements and relations.
distractor_mechanisms: Misconception that larger total transport mass (capacity) implies ability to move larger individual particles, leading students to pick Capacity because Capacity = C * Q (confuses mass rate with size limit).
Attributing particle movement to chemical/dissolved load effects (e.g., 'dissolved load controls binding and release'), a distractor that pulls attention away from hydraulic shear and v^2 dependence.

Assuming capacity and competence scale the same because discharge equals at both sections, concluding 'both equally' despite competence depending on velocity squared and capacity depending only on discharge.

non_obvious_decisions: Recognize that capacity (mass/time) and competence (maximum particle size) are distinct physical quantities and must be compared via the provided numeric relations rather than definitions alone.
Use the given area and velocity values to compute discharge and thus demonstrate equality of capacity across sections, eliminating capacity as the differentiator.
Apply the competence formula to compute D_max values and interpret units (mm) to compare particle sizes directly.

prompt: A town pumps continuously from a single production well screened in a homogeneous, unconfined sand aquifer. Pumping produces a cone of depression in the water table centered on the well. Which single change would most increase the maximum depth (central drawdown) of that cone of depression?

choices.A: Increase the steady pumping rate of the well by a factor of two.
choices.B: Double the aquifer's hydraulic conductivity (K) everywhere.
choices.C: Double the regional recharge rate (R) from rainfall everywhere.
choices.D: Increase the wellbore radius (well casing diameter) by a factor of two while keeping pump rate the same.

solution: Central drawdown depends primarily on the balance between pumping rate and the aquifer's ability to supply water. Doubling the pumping rate doubles the volume removed per time, increasing the head loss near the well and thus increasing central drawdown. Doubling hydraulic conductivity would allow water to flow toward the well more easily and therefore reduce drawdown. Doubling regional recharge likewise supplies more water and reduces drawdown. Increasing wellbore radius (when small relative to the cone) affects only the very near-well flow and has negligible effect on the aquifer-scale maximum drawdown. Therefore option A most increases central drawdown.

reasoning_plan.target_skill: predict how changes in pumping rate and aquifer properties affect drawdown (cone of depression) in an unconfined aquifer
reasoning_plan.novel_context: A town draws water from a single production well in a homogeneous, unconfined sand aquifer. Continuous pumping produces a cone of depression in the water table near the well.
fixed_givens: Aquifer is homogeneous, unconfined, and sand-dominated.
The well pumps continuously at a steady rate.
Hydraulic conductivity (K) and recharge rate (R) are spatially uniform away from the well.
Drawdown (depth of water-table lowering at a given location) increases with greater local extraction relative to the aquifer's ability to transmit water.
Well radius and pump screen geometry are small compared to the scale of the cone of depression.
reasoning_plan.question: Which single change would most increase the maximum depth (central drawdown) of the cone of depression produced by the well?

choices.A: Increase the steady pumping rate of the well by a factor of two.
choices.B: Double the aquifer's hydraulic conductivity (K) everywhere.
choices.C: Double the regional recharge rate (R) from rainfall everywhere.
choices.D: Increase the wellbore radius (well casing diameter) by a factor of two while keeping pump rate the same.

reasoning_plan.explanation_brief: Central drawdown is most sensitive to pumping rate; increasing K or recharge reduces drawdown, and changing well radius (small-scale) has little effect on maximum drawdown at the aquifer scale.

Higher pumping rate increases volume removed per time, increasing drawdown near the well.
Higher hydraulic conductivity allows water to flow more easily toward the well, reducing drawdown.
Higher regional recharge replenishes the aquifer and reduces drawdown for a given pump rate.
Wellbore radius affects local head very near the pump intake but has negligible effect on aquifer-scale maximum drawdown when the well is small relative to the cone.
Identify which change most increases central drawdown.

verification.calculation: Conceptual: central drawdown scales directly with pumping rate for fixed aquifer properties; doubling pump rate increases drawdown significantly, whereas doubling K or recharge reduces drawdown; changing well radius has negligible large-scale effect.

distractor_mechanisms: Belief that increasing hydraulic conductivity increases drawdown because 'more flow' might be misinterpreted as 'more removal' (incorrect sign of effect).
Assuming greater recharge always increases drawdown by adding water movement (confusing flow magnitude with net balance).
Overestimating the influence of wellbore radius on aquifer-scale drawdown (focusing on local hardware instead of system-scale flux).

event_topic: Science Olympiad Division B Dynamic Planet: Earth's Fresh Waters
prompt: A small, well-mixed temperate lake was monitored for a single 24-hour summer day. Using measured, additive rates for the day: initial dissolved oxygen (DO) = 8.00 mg O2 L^-1; gross primary production (GPP) = +2.00 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1; community respiration (R) = −3.00 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1; sediment oxygen demand (SOD) = −0.50 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1; reaeration = +0.05 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1. Hypoxia is defined as DO < 2.0 mg O2 L^-1. All rates apply uniformly over the 24 h and final DO = initial DO + sum of rates. Based only on these measured terms, select the single best statement about the lake's final DO and hypoxia status.

choices.A: Final DO = 6.55 mg O2 L^-1; lake is not hypoxic (DO ≥ 2.0 mg L^-1).
choices.B: Final DO = 7.00 mg O2 L^-1; lake is not hypoxic (calculation ignores sediment oxygen demand).
choices.C: Final DO ≈ 1.20 mg O2 L^-1; lake is hypoxic (assumes large unmeasured solubility-driven loss).
choices.D: Final DO = 8.05 mg O2 L^-1; lake is not hypoxic (assumes reaeration is +1.05 mg L^-1 day^-1 instead of the measured +0.05).

solution_steps: Compute net change: ΔDO = GPP + R + SOD + reaeration = 2.00 + (−3.00) + (−0.50) + 0.05 = −1.45 mg O2 L^-1.
Final DO = initial DO + ΔDO = 8.00 + (−1.45) = 6.55 mg O2 L^-1, which is ≥ 2.0 mg L^-1, so the lake is not hypoxic.
solution: ΔDO = 2.00 − 3.00 − 0.50 + 0.05 = −1.45 mg O2 L^-1. Final DO = 8.00 − 1.45 = 6.55 mg O2 L^-1. Since 6.55 ≥ 2.0 mg O2 L^-1, the lake is not hypoxic. Therefore choice A is correct.

solution_first_blueprint.target_skill: interpretation and budget-solution for lake dissolved oxygen
solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: A single-day measured oxygen budget for a small temperate lake during summer, with explicit measured rates for photosynthesis, respiration, sediment demand, and reaeration; determine final DO and hypoxia status and select the single correct evidence statement.
fixed_givens: Lake mixed and well-mixed for the day (uniform DO throughout volume).
Initial dissolved oxygen (DO) at start of day = 8.00 mg O2 L^-1.
Measured gross primary production (oxygen production by photosynthesis, integrated daytime) = +2.00 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1.
Measured community respiration (biological O2 consumption, 24 h integrated) = -3.00 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1.
Measured sediment oxygen demand (net O2 flux into sediments) = -0.50 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1.
Measured reaeration (net air–water exchange, positive increases DO) = +0.05 mg O2 L^-1 day^-1 (small and explicitly measured).
Hypoxia definition for this task: DO < 2.0 mg O2 L^-1.
All rates are for the same 24-hour period and are additive; temperature-driven equilibrium saturation effects are not separately applied because reaeration is measured.
assumptions: Rates are linear and apply uniformly over the 24-hour period; final DO = initial DO + sum of the given rate terms.
No other sources/sinks of O2 (e.g., lateral inflow/outflow) are significant.
Units are consistent (mg L^-1 and mg L^-1 day^-1); reporting to two decimal places is sufficient.
solution_steps: Compute net O2 change over the day by summing all budget terms: ΔDO = GPP + R + SOD + reaeration.
Add ΔDO to initial DO to get final DO, compare to hypoxia threshold, and select the option whose numeric final DO and conclusion match that calculation using only the fixed givens.
solution_first_blueprint.expected_answer: Final DO = 6.55 mg O2 L^-1; lake is not hypoxic (DO ≥ 2.0 mg L^-1). Correct multiple-choice option: the one stating final DO = 6.55 mg L^-1 and 'not hypoxic'.
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: All given terms are numeric and additive; ΔDO = 2.00 + (−3.00) + (−0.50) + 0.05 = −1.45 mg L^-1, so final DO = 8.00 − 1.45 = 6.55 mg L^-1. No other plausible combination of terms or interpretations yields a different recomputable final DO or different hypoxia conclusion.
distractor_mechanisms: Misapply temperature-driven solubility: use unstated saturation change to claim large DO loss (ignores measured reaeration and measured rates).
Ignore sediment oxygen demand and sum only photosynthesis and respiration (giving final DO = 7.00 mg L^-1).
Treat reaeration as large positive equilibrating flux instead of the measured small +0.05 mg L^-1 day^-1 (yielding a higher final DO).

non_obvious_decisions: Use of measured reaeration instead of inferring solubility-driven gas loss.
Recognizing all budget terms are additive and the correct sign convention for production (+) and consumption (−).

prompt:
Two small inland ponds, Pond X and Pond Y, sit in the same climate on similar geologic substrate. Pond X receives most input from direct precipitation and surface runoff during and immediately after storms. Pond Y receives most input from groundwater seepage (subsurface flow that emerges into the pond). Neither pond has substantial stream inflow or outflow; both lose water similarly by evaporation and seepage.

Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

I. Pond X will show larger short-term water-level increases immediately after a heavy rainstorm than Pond Y.
II. Pond Y will have a higher average dissolved mineral (solute) concentration than Pond X.

A: I only
B: II only
C: I and II
D: Neither I nor II
solution: Precipitation and runoff arrive quickly during/just after storms, so Pond X experiences larger short-term rises in water level than a pond fed mainly by steady groundwater seepage → I is true. Groundwater typically acquires more dissolved minerals through prolonged contact with soils and rock, while precipitation has low solute content → Pond Y should have higher average dissolved mineral concentration → II is true. Therefore both statements are supported.

reasoning_plan.target_skill: distinguish primary water-source effects on short-term water-level variability and dissolved mineral concentration
reasoning_plan.novel_context: Two small inland ponds, Pond X and Pond Y, in the same climate and on similar substrates. Pond X receives most of its input directly from precipitation (rain and snow) and surface runoff after storms. Pond Y receives most of its input from groundwater seepage (subsurface flow emerging into the pond). Neither pond has significant inflow or outflow streams; evaporation and seepage losses are similar for both ponds.
fixed_givens: Precipitation input to a pond typically arrives quickly during and immediately after storms, producing rapid short-term increases in pond water level.
Groundwater inflow to a pond is typically steadier (more constant) over short timescales because it is buffered by subsurface storage.
Groundwater has longer contact time with subsurface rocks and soils and therefore generally carries higher dissolved mineral (solute) concentrations than direct precipitation.
Precipitation (rain/snow) has relatively low dissolved mineral concentration compared to typical groundwater.
reasoning_plan.question:
Given the context above, which of the following conclusions is best supported?

I. Pond X will show larger short-term water-level increases immediately after a heavy rainstorm than Pond Y.
II. Pond Y will have a higher average dissolved mineral (solute) concentration than Pond X.

Choices:
A: I only
B: II only
C: I and II
D: Neither I nor II

nodes.label: Pond X input = precipitation and surface runoff (arrives quickly during storms)
Pond Y input = groundwater seepage (steady, buffered input)
Quick storm-delivered input causes rapid short-term water-level rise
Groundwater has higher dissolved mineral concentration due to rock/soil contact time
Evaluate I: short-term water-level response (Pond X vs Pond Y)
Evaluate II: average dissolved mineral concentration (Pond X vs Pond Y)

distractor_mechanisms: Mistakenly assuming precipitation water always has higher mineral content than groundwater (leads to choosing I only or Neither).
Confusing short-term variability with long-term variability and assuming groundwater-fed pond responds more to storms (leads to choosing II only or Neither).
Assuming both ponds have identical inputs despite given source differences, selecting Neither.

prompt: You are advising managers of a small dimictic recreational lake (area = 0.5 km^2; mean depth = 3.0 m). Late-summer stratified pre-dawn bottom DO has averaged 1.5 mg/L and is hypoxic (<2.0 mg/L) in 6 of the last 10 summers. Current annual total phosphorus (TP) load = 60 kg/yr with sources: septic = 30 kg/yr, agriculture = 18 kg/yr, background/atmospheric = 12 kg/yr. You may choose a single management action to implement now. Assumptions: (1) If installed and operated, continuous aeration will maintain bottom DO >2.5 mg/L during late-summer stratified conditions in each summer it runs. (2) Watershed repairs (septic −80% and agricultural BMPs −50%) immediately lower external TP by 33 kg/yr (new external TP = 27 kg/yr). (3) Internal sediment P can sustain summer algal production so reductions in external TP may not produce proportional, immediate reductions in summer hypoxia; ecological/internal-loading lag of ≥2 years is possible. Objective time window = next 5 years: reduce the frequency of pre-dawn bottom hypoxia (fewer summers with bottom DO <2.0 mg/L across that 5-year period). Which single action most reliably meets the objective over the next 5 years?

choices.A: Install and operate continuous bottom aeration beginning now.
choices.B: Implement watershed repairs now (septic −80% and agricultural BMPs −50%) to reduce external TP immediately.
choices.C: Do nothing now; continue monitoring for another 5 years and reassess.
choices.D: Implement the watershed repairs now but delay installing aeration until the nutrient reductions have been observed.

solution_steps: 1) Determine which action gives an immediate, reliable increase in bottom DO during late-summer stratification across the 5-year window.
2) Compare immediate aeration benefit versus nutrient-reduction benefit that is delayed/uncertain due to internal P lag; choose the action that most reliably reduces hypoxic summers within 5 years.
solution: Given the objective strictly limited to reducing the number of summers with pre-dawn bottom DO <2.0 mg/L over the next 5 years, compare the two feasible interventions. Data: lake area = 0.5 km^2, mean depth = 3.0 m, current late-summer pre-dawn bottom DO = 1.5 mg/L (hypoxic) in 6 of last 10 summers. External TP = 60 kg/yr (septic 30, agriculture 18, background 12). Assumptions: aeration, if operated, will maintain bottom DO >2.5 mg/L each summer it runs (immediate, reliable elimination of hypoxia for those summers). Watershed repairs reduce external TP by 33 kg/yr (to 27 kg/yr) immediately, but internal sediment P can sustain summer algal production and oxygen demand such that hypoxia may persist for multiple years (lag ≥2 years), so there is no guaranteed reduction in hypoxic-summer frequency within the 5-year objective window. Options analysis: A (aeration) directly and immediately addresses the measured symptom (pre-dawn bottom hypoxia) and thus will reliably reduce the count of hypoxic summers in any summers it operates. B (watershed repairs) reduces external loading and is beneficial long-term but, because of internal P and ecological lag, cannot be relied on to reduce hypoxic-summer frequency within the 5-year window. C (do nothing) yields no change. D (repair now but delay aeration) forfeits the immediate DO benefit and relies on a delayed nutrient response. Therefore the single action that uniquely and most reliably meets the time-bounded objective is A: install and operate continuous bottom aeration beginning now.

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: management choice for a small dimictic recreational lake with documented late-summer bottom hypoxia and quantified external TP sources
fixed_givens: Lake area = 0.5 km^2; mean depth = 3.0 m; dimictic
Pre-dawn bottom DO average in late-summer stratified conditions = 1.5 mg/L (hypoxia < 2.0 mg/L)
Hypoxic bottom conditions occurred in 6 of last 10 summers
Annual total phosphorus (TP) load = 60 kg/yr (septic = 30 kg/yr, agriculture = 18 kg/yr, background/atmospheric = 12 kg/yr)
Objective time window = next 5 years; objective = reduce the long-term frequency of pre-dawn bottom hypoxia (fewer summers with bottom DO < 2.0 mg/L across that 5-year period)
Management choices limited to a single action now
assumptions: Installed continuous aeration, if operated, will maintain bottom DO > 2.5 mg/L during late-summer stratified conditions for each summer it runs
Watershed repairs reduce external TP immediately at the watershed outlet by the stated fractions (septic −80%, agricultural −50%), giving external TP reduction = 33 kg/yr (new external TP = 27 kg/yr)

Internal phosphorus (legacy in sediments) can sustain summer algal production such that reductions in external TP may not produce a proportional, immediate reduction in hypoxia within 5 years (typical internal-loading lag of ≥2 years is possible)
Operational costs and maintenance needs for aeration are feasible but require continuous operation to sustain DO benefit
solution_steps: Evaluate direct, time-bounded effect on the objective: aeration immediately raises bottom DO each summer it operates; therefore it will reduce the number of hypoxic summers within the 5-year window while operating.

Evaluate watershed-source action: repairing septic/ag BMPs reduces external TP by 33 kg/yr (from 60 to 27 kg/yr), which reduces external loading but may not promptly convert to reduced summer hypoxia because internal loading and ecological lag can sustain low bottom DO for multiple years.

Compare tradeoffs: aeration provides prompt, reliable mitigation of hypoxia but requires continuous operation and costs; watershed controls reduce external TP long-term and are more sustainable but have delayed and uncertain 5-year hypoxia outcomes due to internal loading.
Select the single action that is uniquely defensible for maximizing fewer hypoxic summers within the specified 5-year period given the monitoring evidence and source-load reductions.
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: Given the objective strictly limited to reducing the frequency of pre-dawn bottom hypoxia across the next 5 years, the aeration choice (A) is uniquely supported: aeration produces an immediate and predictable increase in bottom DO >2.5 mg/L while operating, directly addressing hypoxia each summer in the 5-year window. The watershed TP reductions (B) reduce external load by 33 kg/yr but, because internal sediment P can sustain oxygen demand and produce a multi-year ecological lag, there is no guaranteed reduction in hypoxic-summer frequency within the 5-year objective; doing nothing (C) yields no change; combining delayed source control with postponed implementation (D) forfeits the immediate DO benefit. Thus only A reliably meets the time-bounded objective without adding an ad hoc reliability assumption.
distractor_mechanisms: Assuming external TP reduction immediately and proportionally reduces summer hypoxia (overlooks internal P and ecological lag)
Believing that any single watershed intervention is sufficient within a short 5-year window regardless of legacy P stores
Equating monitoring continuity (do-nothing) with management efficacy—thinking more data replaces immediate remediation

non_obvious_decisions: Model selection: immediate physical oxygenation (aeration) vs. nutrient-load reduction with ecological lag
Interpreting monitoring evidence (frequency and magnitude of hypoxia) to prioritize immediate effect over longer-term sustainability

prompt: On a topographic map, Point A has elevation 340 m and Point B has elevation 180 m. The measured distance along the stream between A and B on the map is 8.0 cm. The map scale is 1:50,000 (1 cm on map = 50,000 cm on ground). Using the vertical difference between A and B as the total channel drop and the map-measured channel length as the horizontal distance, compute the channel gradient expressed as (vertical drop / horizontal distance) × 100%. Give your answer as a percent.
solution_steps: Compute vertical drop: 340 m − 180 m = 160 m.
Convert map distance to ground distance: 8.0 cm × 50,000 cm/cm = 400,000 cm = 4000 m.
Compute percent gradient: (160 m / 4000 m) × 100% = 4%.
solution: Vertical drop = 340 m − 180 m = 160 m. Map distance 8.0 cm at 1:50,000 → ground distance = 8.0 × 50,000 cm = 400,000 cm = 4000 m. Gradient = (160 m / 4000 m) × 100% = 0.04 × 100% = 4%.
rubric: 1 point: Correct calculation of vertical drop (160 m) and correct conversion of 8.0 cm at 1:50,000 to 4000 m.
1 point: Correct computation and reporting of channel gradient as (160 m / 4000 m) × 100% = 4%.

Use measured map channel length as the planimetric horizontal distance along the channel projected onto the map (no correction for channel sinuosity in 3D).
Express channel gradient as (vertical drop / horizontal distance) × 100%.
solution_steps: Compute vertical drop: 340 m − 180 m = 160 m.
Convert map distance to ground distance: 8.0 cm × 50,000 cm/cm = 400,000 cm = 4000 m.
Compute percent gradient: (160 m / 4000 m) × 100% = 4%.
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: Given the fixed elevations, map distance, and scale with the stated assumptions, the calculation yields a single numeric percent value (160 m drop over 4000 m horizontal) so the result is uniquely determined.
distractor_mechanisms: Forgetting to convert map cm to ground meters (e.g., using 8.0 cm as 8.0 m gives 2000% error).
Using elevation values incorrectly (e.g., dividing the higher elevation by distance instead of the drop).
Reporting gradient as a unitless ratio (0.04) instead of percent (4%).

non_obvious_decisions: Interpreting map-measured channel length as the horizontal planimetric distance to use in gradient calculation (rather than true 3D channel length).

prompt: A closed karst basin receives a measured, steady glacial-melt inflow Q_in = 0.45 m^3/s. Over a 2.00-hour observation the basin water level (horizontal planform area A = 20,000 m^2) rises by Δh = 0.12 m. Assume negligible precipitation, evaporation, and other lateral groundwater fluxes, and that Q_in and the unmeasured conduit outflow Q_out are approximately steady during the interval. Using mass continuity (Q_in − Q_out = dS/dt) and ΔS = A·Δh, determine Q_out (m^3/s). Give your answer to two significant figures.
solution_steps: Convert Δt to seconds: Δt = 2.00 h = 2.00 × 3600 = 7200 s.
Compute storage change: ΔS = A · Δh = 20,000 m^2 × 0.12 m = 2400 m^3.
Compute storage rate: dS/dt = ΔS / Δt = 2400 m^3 / 7200 s = 0.333333... m^3/s.
Apply mass continuity Q_in − Q_out = dS/dt → Q_out = Q_in − dS/dt = 0.45 − 0.333333... = 0.116666... m^3/s.
Round to two significant figures: Q_out ≈ 0.12 m^3/s.
rubric: 1 point: Correctly compute storage rate dS/dt = ΔS/Δt = 0.333 m^3/s (or equivalent to three significant figures).
1 point: Correctly apply mass continuity and report Q_out = Q_in − dS/dt ≈ 0.12 m^3/s.

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: A karst spring fed by a measured glacial melt inflow into a closed karst basin whose water level rises during a 2-hour observation; use mass continuity to infer unmeasured conduit outflow.
fixed_givens: measured inflow (glacial melt) Q_in = 0.45 m^3/s (assumed constant during observation)
basin planform area A = 20,000 m^2 (horizontal projection of storage area)
observed storage-level rise Δh = 0.12 m over Δt = 2.00 hours
no measured precipitation or evaporation during the observation period (assume negligible)
seek unmeasured conduit outflow Q_out (m^3/s)
assumptions: Mass continuity applies: Q_in - Q_out = dS/dt, where S is basin storage volume
Storage volume change ΔS = A·Δh (basin area is horizontal and constant with water level change)
Negligible lateral/groundwater fluxes other than the conduit and measured inflow during Δt
Q_in and Q_out are approximately steady over the 2.00 h interval
solution_steps: Convert observation time to seconds: Δt = 2.00 h = 2.00·3600 = 7200 s.
Compute storage volume change: ΔS = A·Δh = 20,000 m^2 · 0.12 m = 2400 m^3.
Compute storage rate: dS/dt = ΔS/Δt = 2400 m^3 / 7200 s = 0.333333... m^3/s.
Apply mass continuity to solve for Q_out: Q_out = Q_in - dS/dt = 0.45 - 0.333333... = 0.116666... m^3/s.
Report Q_out with stated assumptions and appropriate significant figures.
solution_first_blueprint.expected_answer: Q_out = 0.12 m^3/s. (Calculation: ΔS = 20,000·0.12 = 2400 m^3; dS/dt = 2400/7200 = 0.333 m^3/s; Q_out = 0.45 − 0.333 = 0.117 ≈ 0.12 m^3/s. Assumptions: negligible evap/precip, no other fluxes, constant rates.)
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: Given the fixed numerical inflow, basin area, observed rise, and the mass-continuity relation with the stated assumptions, the computed Q_out is uniquely determined; alternative values would require changing an explicit assumption (e.g., adding unmeasured fluxes or nonconstant Q_in).
distractor_mechanisms: Sign error: computing Q_out = Q_in + dS/dt (incorrectly adding storage increase rather than subtracting), yielding ≈0.78 m^3/s.
Unit/time conversion error: using Δt = 2 (hours) as seconds directly, producing an enormous dS/dt and thus negative or zero Q_out.
Using depth change as a flow rate directly (e.g., treating Δh = 0.12 m as m/s) instead of converting to volume change via area.

non_obvious_decisions: Selecting mass continuity (Q_in - Q_out = dS/dt) as the governing relation rather than applying hydraulic formulas
Interpreting basin area as planform area to convert depth change to volume change
Neglecting evap/precip and other fluxes as justified simplifications for a Division B foundational task

prompt: In the same channel, two prior steady-flow observations relate average velocity v (m/s) to the measured maximum movable grain diameter D_max (m) by a power-law D_max ∝ v^n with n constant. Observation 1: v1 = 0.50 m/s, D1 = 0.0075 m. Observation 2: v2 = 1.00 m/s, D2 = 0.030 m. After a storm the channel has a new steady average velocity v3 = 1.60 m/s (all other conditions unchanged). Using the power-law scaling inferred from the two observations, predict the maximum movable grain diameter D3 (in meters) for v3. Give the numeric answer only (SI units).
givens: Assumption: D_max ∝ v^n with n constant
solution_steps: Infer exponent n from observations: D2/D1 = (v2/v1)^n ⇒ 0.030/0.0075 = (1.00/0.50)^n ⇒ 4 = 2^n ⇒ n = 2.
rubric: 1 point: Correctly infer n = 2 from the ratio of observations (show D2/D1 = (v2/v1)^n and solve for n).
1 point: Correct numeric calculation of D3 = 0.0768 m using D3 = D2*(v3/v2)^2.

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: Predict maximum movable grain size for a new steady flow using an empirically inferred scaling between velocity and maximum grain diameter from two prior observations in the same channel.
fixed_givens: Observation 1: average flow velocity v1 = 0.50 m/s, measured maximum movable grain diameter D1 = 7.5 mm (0.0075 m).
Observation 2: average flow velocity v2 = 1.00 m/s, measured maximum movable grain diameter D2 = 30 mm (0.030 m).
New case: average flow velocity v3 = 1.60 m/s at the same cross section after a storm.
Channel slope, grain density, and all other conditions are unchanged between observations and the new case.
assumptions: A single power-law scaling relates maximum movable grain diameter D_max to average velocity v: D_max ∝ v^n, with n constant for this channel and grain population.
Measurement uncertainty is negligible for the purpose of a single best numeric prediction.
Mobilization criterion and grain-size definition are consistent across observations.
solution_steps: Infer exponent n from the two observations: D2/D1 = (v2/v1)^n ⇒ 0.030/0.0075 = (1.00/0.50)^n ⇒ 4 = 2^n ⇒ n = 2.
Apply the inferred scaling to predict D3: D3 = D2 * (v3/v2)^2 = 0.030 m * (1.60/1.00)^2 = 0.030 m * 2.56 = 0.0768 m.
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: Exponent n is uniquely determined (n=2) by the ratio 4 = (1.00/0.50)^n; applying that exact power-law to the single new velocity yields a single numeric D3 = 0.0768 m with no remaining free parameters.
distractor_mechanisms: Assume linear proportionality (n=1) between D_max and v, producing D3 = 0.048 m (mistake: forget nonlinear scaling).
Assume cube scaling (n=3) or another arbitrary exponent, producing D3 = 0.1229 m for n=3 (mistake: mis-infer exponent from data).
Use the smaller observation as baseline but invert ratios incorrectly (e.g., compute D3 = D1*(v3/v1)^2 with unit errors or rounding to 0.08 m) leading to small numeric rounding variants.

non_obvious_decisions: Select a power-law model form D_max ∝ v^n rather than linear or other functional forms.
Solve for the exponent n from two empirical observations.

prompt: A rural spring is fed by a nearby unconfined sand aquifer. Initial local water-table elevation = 150.0 m (above datum). Spring outlet elevation = 145.0 m; the spring flows while the water table is ≥ 145.0 m and stops only when the water table is < 145.0 m. A proposed irrigation well 200 m away will lower the water table at the spring by 0.02 m for every 1.0 L/s of continuous pumping (linear proportionality). Assuming no other changes and sustained pumping long enough to reach steady drawdown, what is the smallest integer continuous pumping rate (in L/s) from the new well that will cause the spring to stop flowing?
solution_steps: Compute required drop: initial water table 150.0 m must be lowered to <145.0 m → required drop > 5.0 m.
Use proportionality 0.02 m drop per 1 L/s: 0.02·r > 5.0 → r > 250 L/s. Smallest integer exceeding 250 is 251 L/s.
solution: Initial water-table elevation = 150.0 m; spring outlet = 145.0 m, so the water table must drop by more than 5.0 m to be <145.0 m. Drawdown at spring = 0.02 m per 1 L/s, so required pumping r satisfies 0.02·r > 5.0 → r > 250 L/s. The smallest integer L/s greater than 250 is 251 L/s, so 251 L/s is the minimum integer continuous rate that will cause the spring to stop.

solution_first_blueprint.novel_context: A rural spring fed by a nearby unconfined sand aquifer is observed to flow only while the local water table is at or above the spring outlet elevation. A new irrigation well 200 m away will lower the water table at the spring by 0.02 m for every 1.0 L/s of continuous pumping.
fixed_givens: Initial local water-table elevation = 150.0 m (above datum).
Spring outlet elevation = 145.0 m; spring flows while water table ≥ 145.0 m and stops when water table < 145.0 m.
Pumping drawdown at the spring = 0.02 m per 1.0 L/s of continuous pumping from the new well (linear proportionality).
Distance 200 m (given but already incorporated in proportional drawdown coefficient).
assumptions: Drawdown scales linearly with pumping rate at the spring location for the relevant range.
No other temporal or seasonal changes in recharge or other pumping occur during continuous pumping.
Pumping is sustained long enough for the steady drawdown at the spring to be realized.
solution_steps: Compute required drop in water table to reduce it from 150.0 m to below 145.0 m. Required drop > 5.0 m (strict inequality because at 145.0 m the spring still flows).

Use proportionality 0.02 m drop per 1 L/s to find pumping rate r satisfying 0.02·r > 5.0 → r > 250 L/s. Therefore the minimum continuous pumping rate that will cause the spring to stop is any rate just above 250 L/s; the smallest integer L/s exceeding 250 is 251 L/s.
solution_first_blueprint.uniqueness_check: The linear proportional model and the strict inequality (water table must be <145.0 m) yield r > 250 L/s uniquely; any r ≤ 250 L/s leaves the water table ≥145.0 m so the spring still flows.
distractor_mechanisms: Using a non-strict inequality (taking required drop = 5.0 m) and selecting 250 L/s (incorrectly treating equality as sufficient to stop flow).
Mistakenly rounding or truncating the proportional calculation to a nearest common choice like 200 or 300 L/s without recognizing the strict >250 threshold.
Confusing elevation drop with absolute elevation and selecting a value that would lower the table to 145.0 m (250 L/s) assuming that equals stopping the spring.

non_obvious_decisions: Recognizing the strict inequality: spring stops only when water table < outlet elevation (not ≤).
Converting continuous proportional drawdown into a minimum pumping rate and interpreting 'minimum' as smallest value that satisfies strict inequality (must exceed 250 L/s).
